standard.title: Critique health information and media
standard.description: critique health information, services and media messaging about relationships, lifestyle choices, health decisions and behaviours to evaluate their influence on individual attitudes and actions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can plan, rehearse and evaluate strategies for managing health and safety risk situations (AC9HP10P08), and have previously investigated how media and influential people impact health attitudes and behaviours (AC9HP8P09). At Y9-10 the focus shifts to critique — a higher-order evaluative move that assesses the validity, bias and influence of health information and media.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students critique health information, services and media messaging to evaluate their influence on attitudes and actions across relationships, lifestyle choices, health decisions and health behaviours.

nodes.label: Criteria for critiquing health information
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify criteria for evaluating the quality, bias and influence of health information and media messaging
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two criteria for evaluating health information (e.g. source credibility, evidence base, whose interests are served) and apply them to one example
nodes.typical_width: Develop criteria for critiquing health information and services; apply criteria to evaluate health information targeting specific groups of young people (substance use, healthy food choices, fitness plans, mental health support, sexual health, personal safety); evaluate strategies and actions to increase personal safety
wider: Analyse the nutritional composition of foods eaten by First Peoples of Australia and evaluate how this information could be used to increase health benefits for everyone — assess how this knowledge has been presented in mainstream health media

Investigate health issues specific to First Nations Australian communities and critique mainstream health messaging for its relevance and accessibility — propose proactive community strategies for promoting better access and health outcomes

Critique health information targeting specific cultural or demographic groups (e.g. young men, LGBTIQ+ youth, culturally and linguistically diverse communities) — evaluate whether the information addresses actual barriers to health access
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify criteria for evaluating health information cannot apply critique in Node 2 — critique requires a principled basis, not just personal opinion about whether information seems right.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly express opinions about health information without applying evaluative criteria — saying a source is unreliable without specifying why by what standard. The investment is in building the criteria explicitly first: what makes health information credible, what indicates bias, what does it mean to evaluate whose interests a message serves. These criteria then underpin the critique work in Node 2.

success_criteria: Names at least two criteria for evaluating health information quality or bias
Applies criteria to a specific example — not just describes them in the abstract
Criteria include something beyond 'is from a reliable source' — e.g. considers whose interests are served, what is left out, who the audience is

nodes.label: Critiquing media messaging about health
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can critique health information and media messaging to evaluate their influence on attitudes and actions
nodes.minimum_width: Critique one piece of health information or media messaging — apply criteria to evaluate its quality, identify its likely influence on attitudes, and explain what it leaves out
nodes.typical_width: Critique health information and services across multiple domains (substance use, food, fitness, mental health, sexual health, personal safety); critique how the portrayal of sexual relationships in TV, advertisements, movies, popular music and online content may influence beliefs about respectful, safe and consensual relationships; evaluate influence on individual attitudes and actions
wider: Critique a specific media portrayal of sexual relationships (film, TV, pornography, advertising) using evidence-based criteria for respectful and consensual relationships — evaluate the gap between the portrayal and legal/ethical standards
Investigate and critique a health campaign targeting a specific community — evaluate whether it is culturally appropriate, accessible, and likely to achieve its stated goals
Design a counter-messaging strategy for a specific piece of misleading health information — evaluate what approach would most effectively reach the target audience

response_modes.reason: Health media critique requires practice across different domains and message types — food advertising operates differently from sexual health messaging in social media, which operates differently from a government health campaign. Students need to apply their criteria across multiple message types to develop genuine critique capability. The sexual relationships media direction is particularly important given the elaborations' explicit inclusion of pornography and its influence on consent beliefs.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Sexual relationships media critique, targeted community health campaign evaluation, and counter-messaging design each require applying critique capability in a substantially different context. Students who engage the wider tier develop critique as a genuinely transferable skill rather than competence with one message type.
success_criteria: Applies specific criteria (from Node 1) to critique a named piece of health information or media
Evaluates the likely influence on attitudes or actions — not just the quality of the information itself
Identifies what is absent or distorted in the message, not only what it gets wrong
